blocks.text:
A single Redis server is a single point of failure. If the machine dies, the process crashes, or someone runs a bad deployment, every key in memory is gone until you restore from disk, and during that time every service that depends on Redis is degraded. Even when nothing fails, one server has limits: one CPU core executes commands, and the network card of that one machine serves every read.

**Replication** is the oldest and simplest answer to both problems. You run one **primary** (the older docs and some tools say "master") that accepts writes, and one or more **replicas** (older name: "slaves") that keep a live copy of the primary's data. Replicas are a safety net, a way to spread read traffic, and the building block for everything else in this Part: Sentinel promotes replicas automatically, and Redis Cluster gives every shard its own replicas.

This chapter explains exactly how the copy is made and kept up to date, what the copy does and does not guarantee, and how to read from replicas without being surprised.

blocks.text:
Three facts explain almost everything about Redis replication:

1. **Replication is asynchronous.** The primary executes your write, replies `OK` to the client, and only then (a few microseconds or milliseconds later) sends the command to the replicas. The client is not waiting for the replicas.
2. **A replica is a byte-for-byte follower of a command stream.** The primary turns every write into a replication stream (the same RESP format clients use) and sends it to each replica, which applies it in order. A replica never decides anything on its own about the data.
3. **Replication is one-directional.** Data flows primary → replica. By default a replica is read-only and rejects writes.

The second fact has a useful consequence: two instances that have the same *replication ID* and the same *replication* *offset* hold exactly the same data. We will use that pair in a moment.

### Setting up a replica

You turn any Redis server into a replica of another with one command, at runtime, without restarting:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6380> REPLICAOF 127.0.0.1 6379
OK
127.0.0.1:6380> SET x 1
(error) READONLY You can't write against a read only replica.
blocks.title: Make a server a replica

blocks.text:
The equivalent line in `redis.conf` is `replicaof 127.0.0.1 6379`. To turn a replica back into a standalone primary (this is what a manual failover does), run `REPLICAOF NO ONE`. The older command name `SLAVEOF` still works as an alias, but use `REPLICAOF` in everything you write.

If the primary requires authentication, the replica needs credentials too: `masterauth <password>` (and `masteruser` `<name>` when you use ACL users). Forgetting this is the most common reason a new replica sits in a connecting state forever; the replica's log shows an authentication error.

You can inspect the relationship from either side with `INFO replication` and `ROLE`:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO replication
# Replication
role:master
connected_slaves:1
slave0:ip=127.0.0.1,port=6380,state=online,offset=101,lag=1
master_failover_state:no-failover
master_replid:bda517231b38b6332e881849b0a973f186e557eb
master_replid2:0000000000000000000000000000000000000000
master_repl_offset:101
second_repl_offset:-1
repl_backlog_active:1
repl_backlog_size:1048576
repl_backlog_first_byte_offset:1
repl_backlog_histlen:101
127.0.0.1:6379> ROLE
1) "master"
2) (integer) 101
3) 1) 1) "127.0.0.1"
      2) "6380"
      3) "101"
blocks.title: Inspecting replication (typical output, trimmed)

blocks.text:
The field names still use the old words (`connected_slaves`, `slave0`) for compatibility with tools that parse the output. Read them as replicas. Compare `master_repl_offset` on the primary with the replica's `slave_repl_offset`: the difference, in bytes of replication stream, is the replica's lag. The `lag=1` in the `slave0` line is a different measure: seconds since the replica last acknowledged.

### Full synchronization

When a replica connects for the first time (or after it has been away too long), it needs a complete copy of the dataset. This is a **full resynchronization**:

1. The replica sends `PSYNC ? -1`, which means "I have no history, give me everything".
2. The primary replies with `+FULLRESYNC <replid> <offset>` and starts a background save (a `fork`, exactly like `BGSAVE`; see the chapter on RDB snapshots in Part 4) to produce an RDB snapshot.
3. While the snapshot is being produced and transferred, the primary keeps accepting writes and **buffers** them in memory in a per-replica output buffer.
4. The replica receives the RDB file, flushes its old dataset, and loads the snapshot into memory. While it does this it cannot serve fresh data.
5. The primary then sends the buffered writes, and from then on streams every new write as it happens.

This works on any primary, but it is expensive: a fork on the primary, a burst of network traffic proportional to the dataset size, a load on the replica, and a memory cost for the buffered writes. On a 20 GB dataset this takes minutes.

#### Disk-backed versus diskless

By default the primary can write the RDB to its disk and then send the file (disk-backed), or it can have the forked child **stream the RDB straight to the replica sockets** without touching disk (diskless). Diskless is the default in recent versions (`repl-diskless-sync yes`). Because a diskless transfer to several replicas is more efficient when they arrive together, the primary waits `repl-diskless-sync-delay` seconds (default 5) after the first replica asks, to collect more replicas before it starts the transfer. Set it to 0 if you have only one replica and do not want to wait. On the replica side, `repl-diskless-load` controls whether the replica parses the RDB directly from the socket instead of saving it to disk first; the default is `disabled`, and the other values (`swapdb`, `on-empty-db`) trade extra memory or risk for speed, so leave it alone until you have measured a real problem.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Diskless replication removes the primary's *disk* from the sync path, not the fork. The child process still needs copy-on-write memory while the primary takes writes, so keep memory headroom (see the chapter on RDB snapshots).

### Partial resynchronization

Networks blip. If every disconnection triggered a full sync, a ten-second network glitch would cost you a fork and gigabytes of traffic. Redis avoids this with **partial resynchronization** (`PSYNC`).

Three pieces make it work:

- **Replication ID (**`replid`**)**: a long random string that names one *history* of the dataset. A primary generates a new one when it starts fresh or when a replica is promoted.
- **Replication offset**: a number that increases by the number of bytes of replication stream the primary produces. It increases even when no replica is connected.
- **Replication backlog**: a fixed-size in-memory ring buffer on the primary holding the most recent bytes of the stream (`repl-backlog-size`, default 1 MB).

A replica remembers the `replid` and the offset it has processed. When it reconnects it sends `PSYNC <replid>` `<offset+1>`. The primary checks two conditions: it recognises that replication ID, and the requested byte is still inside the backlog. If both hold, it answers `+CONTINUE` and sends only the missing bytes. Otherwise it falls back to a full resync.

blocks.code:
Backlog (ring buffer, size = repl-backlog-size)

  oldest byte kept                                       master_repl_offset
        │                                                       │
        ▼                                                       ▼
        [ ...................... recent stream ...................]
              ▲
              │
   replica offset 400 000  → inside the window → +CONTINUE (partial)
   replica offset  10 000  → already overwritten → full resync

blocks.text:
The default of 1 MB is small. The right size is: *peak write rate (bytes of stream per second) × the longest disconnection* *you want to survive without a full resync*, plus a margin. If your primary produces 5 MB/s of replication stream and you want to ride out a 2 minute outage, you need roughly 600 MB. Memory for the backlog is allocated once and shared by all replicas, so one large backlog costs the same with one replica or ten. If the primary has had no replicas for `repl-backlog-ttl` seconds (default 3600) it frees the backlog.

#### Why there are two replication IDs

After a failover the promoted replica starts a new history, so it picks a new `replid`, but it remembers the old one as `master_replid2` together with the offset at which the switch happened (`second_repl_offset`). The other replicas, which still talk in terms of the old ID, can therefore reconnect to the new primary and get a *partial* sync instead of a full one. Since Redis 4.0 this makes failovers much cheaper: the cost is a few seconds, not a full dataset transfer.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A replica that restarts and loads from an AOF file cannot do a partial sync, because the AOF does not store the replication ID and offset. A replica that restarts with an RDB file can. This is one reason some operators keep replicas on RDB only even when the primary uses AOF.

### What exactly travels on the wire

It helps to know what a replica receives after the initial sync, because it explains several behaviours. The stream is a sequence of ordinary RESP commands, but not always the commands your clients sent:

- **Non-deterministic commands are rewritten.** A command such as `SPOP` removes a random member; replaying it on a replica could remove a different one. The primary therefore propagates the deterministic effect (`SREM` of the member it picked). Relative expiry commands (`EXPIRE key 60`) are propagated as absolute times (`PEXPIREAT`), so a replica that receives them late still expires the key at the same moment.
- **Expiry and eviction become** `DEL`**.** Only the primary decides a key has expired or must be evicted; it then sends an explicit `DEL` (or `UNLINK`).
- **Lua scripts replicate by effect.** Since Redis 5 the default is to send the commands a script executed, not the script text, so scripts may call random or time commands safely.
- **Heartbeats.** The primary sends a `PING` every `repl-ping-replica-period` seconds (default 10), and each replica sends `REPLCONF ACK <offset>` back about once per second. Those acknowledgements are what `WAIT`, `min-replicas-to-write` and the `lag=` field in `INFO` are built on.
- `SELECT` commands are inserted when the stream switches database.

Because the stream is a single ordered sequence applied by a single thread, one slow command on a replica delays everything behind it, and a replica applies writes strictly in the order the primary produced them. That ordering is the reason a replica is always a consistent (if slightly old) snapshot of the primary rather than a random mixture.

### What replication does and does not guarantee

Because the primary replies before the replicas have the write, there is always a window in which a write exists only on the primary. If the primary dies in that window and a replica is promoted, **the write is lost**. In a failover under load this window is usually small (microseconds to milliseconds of stream), but it is not zero, and it grows if a replica is lagging.

Redis gives you two tools to narrow the window. Neither turns Redis into a strongly consistent database.

#### WAIT: ask for acknowledgements

`WAIT numreplicas timeout` blocks the calling client until all previous writes **of this connection** have been acknowledged by at least `numreplicas` replicas, or until `timeout` milliseconds pass. It returns how many replicas acknowledged. A timeout of 0 blocks forever, so use a real number.

The second `WAIT` returned `1` after 100 ms because only one replica is connected. Your code must compare the return value with what it asked for, and decide what to do if the write is under-replicated (retry, log, alert, or fail the request). `WAIT` does not roll anything back. Also, replication being acknowledged in memory does not mean it is on disk: since Redis 7.2 there is a companion command, `WAITAOF numlocal numreplicas timeout`, that waits for writes to be fsynced to the AOF locally and/or on replicas.

Even `WAIT` is best effort in a failover. It makes it more likely that the replica chosen by Sentinel or Cluster has your write, but the promotion logic does not guarantee it.

#### min-replicas-to-write: refuse writes when too few replicas are healthy

The primary can also protect itself. With these two settings it stops accepting writes when too few replicas are healthy:

blocks.code:
min-replicas-to-write 1
min-replicas-max-lag 10
blocks.title: redis.conf (primary)

blocks.text: Replicas send an acknowledgement to the primary about once per second. If fewer than `min-replicas-to-write` replicas have acknowledged within the last `min-replicas-max-lag` seconds, the primary answers write commands with an error (`NOREPLICAS Not enough good replicas to write.`) instead of executing them. This bounds how much data a partitioned or isolated primary can accept (and later lose); we return to this in the Sentinel chapter as a split-brain mitigation. The price is availability: if your only replica is down, the primary stops taking writes. Choose it deliberately.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: **Replication is not a backup.** A bad `FLUSHALL`, a buggy deployment that deletes keys, or a corrupted value is replicated to every replica within milliseconds. You still need RDB/AOF files and tested restores (see the operations Part).

### Reading from replicas

Replicas can serve reads, so adding replicas increases read capacity for read-heavy workloads such as a product catalogue. Two things to understand first.

#### Reads can be stale

A read from a replica reflects the primary as of a moment ago. Usually that is a few milliseconds; under heavy write load, a slow network or a big full sync, it can be seconds. The classic bug is **read-your-writes**: a user updates their profile (goes to the primary), the page reloads (reads from a replica), and the old value appears. Mitigations: read from the primary for a short time after a write by the same user, route all of a session's traffic to the primary for critical flows, or use `WAIT` before redirecting.

#### Expiry on replicas

Replicas do not expire keys on their own. When the primary expires or evicts a key it sends a synthetic `DEL` to the replicas. In between, a replica may still hold a key that is logically expired; to avoid returning it, the replica checks the key's TTL against its own clock and answers "not found" for read commands. One consequence is that if the replica's clock differs from the primary's, TTL behaviour can look different; keep clocks synchronised with NTP. After a replica is promoted it starts expiring keys itself.

#### Other behaviours worth knowing

- `replica-read-only yes` (default) makes replicas reject writes. Writable replicas exist, but data written to them diverges from the primary and is wiped at the next resync. Avoid them.
- `replica-serve-stale-data yes` (default) lets a replica answer reads while its link to the primary is down or while it is doing the initial sync, with whatever it has. Set it to `no` if returning old or empty data is worse than returning an error; the replica then answers most commands with `MASTERDOWN`.
- `replica-priority` (default 100) is used by Sentinel when choosing which replica to promote. A replica with priority 0 is never promoted, which is useful for a reporting replica in another data centre.
- **Chained replication**: a replica can have replicas of its own. This reduces the load on the primary when you have many replicas, at the cost of more lag at the bottom of the chain.
- Containers and NAT: when the primary sees a replica's address as the container or NAT address, Sentinel and tools that read `INFO replication` get wrong endpoints. Set `replica-announce-ip` and `replica-announce-port` on the replica.

For a Spring Boot application using Lettuce, the read preference is a one-line customization (Spring Boot 4 package shown). With a replicated setup (Sentinel or static master/replica configuration), `ReadFrom.REPLICA_PREFERRED` reads from replicas when they are available and from the primary otherwise:

blocks.title: RedisReadConfig.java

blocks.text:
Use this only for reads that tolerate staleness, such as the product catalogue. Writes still go to the primary. The Lettuce chapter in the Java clients Part and the Spring setup chapter explain the other `ReadFrom` choices and how topology changes are handled.

### A dangerous combination: no persistence plus automatic restart

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Suppose the primary has persistence turned off and an init system or orchestrator that restarts crashed processes. The primary crashes and restarts with an **empty dataset**. Its replicas reconnect, see the new empty primary, and faithfully replicate "nothing", deleting their copy of your data. Either keep persistence on in the primary, or disable automatic restart for it (and let Sentinel or an operator promote a replica first).

### Promoting a replica by hand

Sooner or later you move the primary role deliberately: a hardware upgrade, an OS patch, a failed disk. Without Sentinel or Cluster, the steps are manual. The safest sequence stops writes first so that the replica is fully caught up:

1. Make sure the replica is healthy and caught up: `master_link_status:up` and `slave_repl_offset` equal to the primary's `master_repl_offset`.
2. Stop writes (pause the application, or put the primary into maintenance). `CLIENT PAUSE <ms> WRITE` blocks writes for a limited time without disconnecting anyone.
3. Check again that the offsets match, then run `REPLICAOF NO ONE` on the replica.
4. Point the application (or the DNS name or load balancer) at the new primary, and make the old primary a replica of it with `REPLICAOF`.

Since Redis 6.2 there is a command that coordinates this for you. Run it on the **primary**:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:6379> FAILOVER TO 10.0.1.11 6379 TIMEOUT 5000
OK
127.0.0.1:6379> INFO replication
# Replication
role:master
master_failover_state:waiting-for-sync
...
blocks.title: Coordinated failover with FAILOVER

blocks.text:
The primary pauses writes, waits until the chosen replica has caught up to its exact offset, hands over the role, and turns itself into a replica of the new primary. `TIMEOUT` bounds how long it waits, `FORCE` (with `TO`, and `TIMEOUT`) completes the switch even if the replica did not catch up, and `FAILOVER ABORT` cancels one in progress. The `master_failover_state` field you saw in `INFO replication` shows `no-failover`, `waiting-for-sync` or `failover-in-progress`. This is a manual, lossless switch of roles; it is not failure detection, which is what Sentinel adds.

### Monitoring replication

Four checks catch most replication problems before users notice:

rows: `up` means connected; `down` for longer than a few seconds needs investigation (network, auth, primary down)
Lag in bytes of replication stream; a steady increase means the replica cannot keep up
`lag= field per replica on the primary`
Seconds since the last acknowledgement; above the `min-replicas-max-lag` value the primary may refuse writes
Full syncs on a stable system suggest a too-small backlog or flapping links
blocks.caption: Replication signals worth alerting on.

blocks.text:
Byte lag is a more precise health signal than seconds, but remember that both only tell you about the *replication link*. They say nothing about whether the replica's own disk or CPU is the problem; for that use the general monitoring chapter in the operations Part.

### Common replication mistakes

- **Treating a replica as a backup.** It faithfully copies deletions and corruption.
- **Leaving the backlog at 1 MB** on a busy primary, so every short disconnection becomes a full sync.
- **Forgetting** `masterauth` (and `masteruser`) on the replicas, so they cannot sync, or cannot follow a new primary after failover.
- **Reading your own writes from a replica** and being surprised by stale data.
- **Running the primary without persistence under an auto-restarting supervisor**, which can erase the replicas.
- **Writable replicas** used for scratch data, which silently diverge.
- **Counting on** `WAIT` **as consensus.** It tells you how many replicas acknowledged, nothing more.
- **Starting many replicas at once** on a large dataset and saturating the primary's network.
- **Ignoring clocks.** Replica-side logical expiry and TTL reasoning assume reasonably synchronised clocks.

### Replication settings at a glance

rows: Make this node a replica of another
Credentials the replica uses to authenticate to the primary
Child streams the RDB to replicas without writing a file
Seconds to wait for more replicas before starting a diskless transfer
Size of the partial-resync buffer; size it from write rate × outage time
Seconds without replicas before the backlog is freed

### Failure scenarios in practice

#### A replica loses the network for 30 seconds

It reconnects, sends its `replid` and offset, the primary finds those bytes still in the backlog, and a partial sync catches it up in milliseconds. If the primary wrote more than the backlog size in that time, you get a full sync instead. Watch the `sync_full` and `sync_partial_ok` / `sync_partial_err` counters in `INFO stats`: a rising `sync_full` on a stable system means the backlog is too small or the link is flaky.

#### Full sync makes the primary's memory grow

During a full sync the primary buffers new writes for the replica in its client output buffer. If the replica is slow, that buffer can grow large, and `client-output-buffer-limit replica` (default `256mb 64mb 60`) disconnects the replica when it is exceeded, which restarts the sync, which grows the buffer again. This loop is a classic cause of "replica can never finish syncing". Raise the limit, give the replica more CPU and network, or sync it during a quiet period.

#### Many replicas at once

If the primary restarts and ten replicas resync simultaneously, the primary produces one RDB (with diskless sync and its delay, or by sharing a disk-based RDB) but must push it ten times. The network card, not Redis, is the bottleneck. Chained replication or staggered restarts help.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: A typical product-catalogue setup for ShopStream: one primary in the main zone, two replicas in two other availability zones, `min-replicas-to-write` left at 0 because the catalogue is a cache that can be rebuilt, and read traffic from the catalogue service sent to the replicas through the client's `ReadFrom` setting (see the Lettuce chapter). For the order stream, where losing writes hurts, the same topology runs with AOF on and the application uses `WAIT` for the few writes that must survive a failover.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does Redis replication work, and can it lose data? It is asynchronous: the primary applies a write, replies to the client, then streams the write to replicas. A new replica gets a full sync (RDB snapshot via fork, plus buffered writes); a reconnecting replica uses PSYNC with its replication ID and offset to receive only the missing bytes from the primary's backlog. Because the reply precedes the replication, writes that only reached the primary are lost if it fails and a replica is promoted. `WAIT` and `min-replicas-to-write` narrow that window but do not make Redis strongly consistent.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Replication is asynchronous and one-directional: primary → replicas, applied as a command stream.

- Full sync = fork + RDB + buffered writes; partial sync = replication ID + offset + backlog.
- Size `repl-backlog-size` from your write rate and the outage you want to ride out; the 1 MB default is small.
- Replicas can serve reads but those reads can be stale; do not use them for read-your-writes flows.
- `WAIT` and `min-replicas-to-write` reduce, but never eliminate, the window for lost writes.
- Replication is not a backup, and a non-persistent primary that restarts empty can wipe its replicas.

Replication gives you a copy of the data, but not a decision. When the primary dies at 3 a.m., somebody (or something) must notice, choose the best replica, promote it with `REPLICAOF NO ONE`, point the other replicas at it, and tell every client where the new primary lives. Doing that by hand means an outage that lasts as long as it takes a person to wake up and type correctly.

**Redis Sentinel** is a separate, small process (it is the same `redis-server` binary started in sentinel mode, or the `redis-sentinel` command) that automates exactly this. A group of Sentinels watches a primary and its replicas, agrees when the primary is down, elects one Sentinel to run the failover, promotes a replica, and acts as a **service-discovery endpoint**: clients ask Sentinel "who is the primary of `mymaster` right now?" instead of hard-coding an address.

Sentinel does not shard data. Every node still holds the full dataset. Sentinel is high availability for a single shard; if your data does not fit on one machine, you need Redis Cluster (later in this Part).

blocks.text:
A minimal, sensible deployment has:

- one primary and at least one (usually two) replicas, running as ordinary Redis servers;
- **three or more Sentinel processes**, an odd number, placed on **different machines or availability zones**, so that no single failure takes out a majority of them. Putting three Sentinels on one host protects against a Redis crash but not against that host failing, which defeats the purpose.

Sentinels discover each other and the replicas automatically. You only tell each Sentinel where the primary is; it learns the replicas from the primary's `INFO` output and other Sentinels through a Pub/Sub channel on the primary (`__sentinel__:hello`).

### Detecting failure: SDOWN and ODOWN

Every Sentinel sends `PING` to the primary, replicas and other Sentinels once per second. Detection happens in two stages.

1. **Subjectively down (SDOWN).** If one Sentinel gets no valid reply from an instance for `down-after-milliseconds`, it marks it SDOWN. This is a single Sentinel's opinion. It may be the Sentinel that has a network problem, not the primary.
2. **Objectively down (ODOWN).** When a Sentinel sees the primary as SDOWN, it asks the other Sentinels (`SENTINEL` `is-master-down-by-addr`). If at least **quorum** Sentinels agree, the primary is flagged ODOWN and a failover can start.

The **quorum** is the number of Sentinels that must agree the primary is unreachable. This is the point where people get confused, so read this twice: **the quorum is only used to detect the failure.** To actually run a failover, one Sentinel must be elected leader, and that election needs votes from the **majority of all Sentinels** (more than half of those configured), regardless of the quorum setting.

rows: Failure is detected easily, but with 3 Sentinels unreachable no failover can start
Not recommended: losing either one blocks any failover
blocks.caption: Quorum and majority for different Sentinel counts.

blocks.text:
If the Sentinels that can still talk to each other are fewer than the majority, no failover starts. That is the rule that prevents two halves of a partitioned network from both promoting a primary.

### The failover, step by step

1. A Sentinel declares the primary ODOWN (quorum reached) and asks to be leader. Each Sentinel votes once per **configuration epoch** (a monotonically increasing number that versions the configuration). The Sentinel that collects votes from a majority becomes leader for that epoch. If nobody wins, they retry after a randomised delay (the retry interval relates to `failover-timeout`).
2. The leader **selects the best replica**. Replicas that were disconnected from the primary too long are disqualified. The rest are ordered by `replica-priority` (lower is better; priority 0 means never promote), then by replication offset (the one that received the most data wins), then by lexicographically smaller run ID.
3. The leader sends `REPLICAOF NO ONE` to the chosen replica, which becomes the new primary, and waits until it reports role `master`.
4. The leader reconfigures the other replicas to follow the new primary, at most `parallel-syncs` of them at a time, so most replicas keep serving reads while the others resync.
5. The new configuration is published with a higher epoch. All Sentinels adopt the **highest epoch** version of the configuration, which is how they converge on the same view. Sentinel publishes the `+switch-master` event on its Pub/Sub channel with the old and new addresses.
6. When the old primary comes back, Sentinels reconfigure it as a replica of the new primary. It will then do a resync (usually partial, thanks to the second replication ID) and discard any writes it accepted that the new primary never saw.

Typical end-to-end failover time is `down-after-milliseconds` (detection) plus a few seconds for election and promotion. The default `down-after-milliseconds` is 30000 (30 seconds), so out of the box a dead primary is noticed after 30 seconds. Lower values mean faster failover and more false alarms from slow networks, GC-style pauses of the machine, or short blips.

### Configuration

Here is a Sentinel configuration for three Sentinels watching ShopStream's session store. All three use the same file (with their own `port` if they share a host).

blocks.code:
port 26379
sentinel monitor shop-sessions 10.0.1.10 6379 2
sentinel down-after-milliseconds shop-sessions 5000
sentinel failover-timeout shop-sessions 60000
sentinel parallel-syncs shop-sessions 1
sentinel auth-pass shop-sessions s3cr3t-change-me
requirepass sentinel-s3cr3t
blocks.title: sentinel.conf

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `sentinel monitor <name> <ip> <port> <quorum>` is the only mandatory line. The name is how clients refer to the primary; the quorum (2 of 3 here) is for failure detection only.
- Every other option has the form `sentinel <option> <name> <value>`. Defaults are `down-after-milliseconds` `30000`, `failover-timeout 180000` and `parallel-syncs 1`. The `failover-timeout` bounds how long a failover attempt may take and how long Sentinels wait before retrying a failover that failed.
- `sentinel auth-pass` is the password Sentinel uses to log in to the Redis nodes. It must match `requirepass` (or the ACL user, with `sentinel auth-user`) on every node, replicas included, and the replicas need `masterauth` set so they can follow a new primary. Missing `masterauth` on a replica is a very common cause of a failover that "works" but leaves replicas disconnected.
- `requirepass` here protects the Sentinel itself, which clients and other Sentinels connect to on port 26379.

Start a Sentinel with `redis-sentinel /etc/redis/sentinel.conf` (or `redis-server sentinel.conf --sentinel`).

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: **Sentinel rewrites its own configuration file.** It records the replicas and Sentinels it has discovered, the current epoch and the current primary's address into `sentinel.conf`. The file must therefore be writable, and you must not copy a used `sentinel.conf` to a new machine or bake it into an image: duplicated "myid" lines make Sentinels confuse each other. Give each Sentinel a fresh minimal file.
### Asking Sentinel questions

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli -p 26379
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name shop-sessions
1) "10.0.1.10"
2) "6379"
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL replicas shop-sessions
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL sentinels shop-sessions
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL ckquorum shop-sessions
OK 3 usable Sentinels. Quorum and failover authorization can be reached
127.0.0.1:26379> SENTINEL failover shop-sessions
OK
blocks.title: Querying a Sentinel

blocks.text:
`SENTINEL replicas` and `SENTINEL sentinels` list the known nodes with their flags and offsets, `SENTINEL ckquorum` checks that quorum and majority are reachable (run it in monitoring and after changes), and `SENTINEL failover` `<name>` triggers a failover manually, without needing agreement that the primary is down. The latter is the right way to move the primary before maintenance. The older name for the first command's replica listing was `SENTINEL slaves`; the current command is `SENTINEL replicas`.

You can also subscribe to a Sentinel to receive events such as `+sdown`, `+odown`, `+failover-end` and `+switch-master`:

blocks.code:
PSUBSCRIBE *
# +switch-master shop-sessions 10.0.1.10 6379 10.0.1.11 6379

blocks.text:
### Client discovery

Sentinel only works if your clients cooperate. A Sentinel-aware client is configured with the list of Sentinel addresses and the primary's name, never with the primary's address. On startup, and after a connection failure, the client asks a Sentinel `SENTINEL get-master-addr-by-name`, connects to the answer, and verifies that the node reports itself as primary with `ROLE`. A good client also subscribes to `+switch-master` so it reconnects immediately.

In Spring Boot (Lettuce is the default client) this is configuration only:

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      password: s3cr3t-change-me
      sentinel:
        master: shop-sessions
        nodes:
          - 10.0.2.21:26379
          - 10.0.2.22:26379
          - 10.0.2.23:26379
        password: sentinel-s3cr3t
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text:
Notice that `spring.data.redis.password` is for the Redis data nodes and `spring.data.redis.sentinel.password` is for the Sentinels, a distinction that regularly costs an hour. Spring and the Java clients are covered in their own Parts, including how to read from replicas and how clients behave while a failover is in progress (commands fail for a few seconds, so your retry and timeout settings matter).

### Following a failover through its events

Every state change in a failover is published as an event on a Sentinel Pub/Sub channel named after the event, which makes failovers observable and scriptable. You will see these, roughly in this order:

rows: This Sentinel (or enough Sentinels) consider the primary down
This Sentinel wants to run the failover
The leader election and its winner
The replica to promote was chosen
`REPLICAOF NO ONE` was sent and the replica became primary
Other replicas are being pointed to the new primary
The configuration changed: name, old address, new address. The one most applications care about
blocks.caption: Sentinel events in the life of a failover.

blocks.text:
The event names still contain the word `slave` in some places for compatibility. Monitoring tools usually alert on `+odown`, `+switch-master` and on any `-failover-abort-*` events (failover attempts that gave up, for example when no suitable replica exists).

### Operating Sentinel

#### Adding and removing nodes

New replicas need no Sentinel configuration: start them with `replicaof` pointing at the current primary and the Sentinels discover them within seconds. A new Sentinel only needs the same `sentinel monitor` line; it finds the others through the primary's hello channel. When you retire a node, Sentinels remember it as down forever unless you tell them to forget: run `SENTINEL RESET <name>` (or `SENTINEL RESET *`) on each Sentinel to clear stale replicas and Sentinels from its state, one Sentinel at a time with a pause in between. To stop monitoring a primary altogether use `SENTINEL REMOVE <name>`.

#### Changing settings at runtime

`SENTINEL SET <name> down-after-milliseconds 5000` changes a monitored primary's settings on that Sentinel and persists it in the configuration file. Remember that a setting like this is **per Sentinel**: apply it to all of them, or they will disagree. Sentinel-wide parameters can be read and set with `SENTINEL CONFIG GET` and `SENTINEL CONFIG SET` (Redis 6.2 and later).

#### Scripts and notifications

Sentinel can run an executable on events: `sentinel notification-script <name> <path>` is called for warnings (for example `+sdown`, `+odown`) so you can page someone, and `sentinel client-reconfig-script <name> <path>` is called when the primary changes so you can update a DNS record, a load balancer or a configuration store. Scripts must exit quickly, must be executable, and must exit with code 0 on success. In many modern deployments the clients' Sentinel support and the Pub/Sub events replace the need for these scripts, but they remain the way to integrate non-Sentinel-aware software.

#### Security

Sentinels expose the same kind of control-plane commands as Redis servers (including `SENTINEL FAILOVER` and `SENTINEL SET`), so protect them like servers: private network only, `requirepass` or ACLs, TLS if your Redis nodes use it, and no exposure to the internet. A client that can reach and command a Sentinel can redirect all traffic to a server of its choice.

### What your application sees during a failover

From the application's side, a failover is a window of a few seconds in which:

- commands to the old primary time out or fail with connection errors;
- connections to replicas that are being reconfigured drop and reconnect, because they restart a sync;
- `READONLY` errors can appear if a client still talks to an old primary that has been demoted to a replica;
- in-flight writes whose acknowledgement was lost have an unknown outcome: they might have happened, and might not be on the new primary.

A robust application therefore uses command timeouts that are shorter than the user's patience, retries only operations that are **idempotent** (or protects them with idempotency keys; see the idempotency chapter in the Patterns Part), and has a defined degraded mode if Redis is unavailable. The Java clients Part shows how to configure reconnection and timeouts, and the failover test in the Sentinel lab lets you observe all of this with your own eyes.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Teams that run Sentinel in production commonly schedule a **game day**: kill the primary in staging while a load generator runs, and measure three numbers: time until the first successful write on the new primary, how many writes failed, and whether any acknowledged write is missing afterwards. If any of these surprises the team, the application settings (timeouts, retries, idempotency) need work before the next real failure.

### Split brain and what Sentinel cannot promise

Imagine primary P with two replicas, and a network partition that isolates P (and one Sentinel) from the other two Sentinels and the replicas:

blocks.code:
side A                          side B
┌───────────────┐   partition   ┌──────────────────────────┐
│  P (primary)  │      ╳        │ R1, R2 (replicas)        │
│  Sentinel S1  │               │ Sentinel S2, S3          │
│  clients X    │               │ clients Y                │
└───────────────┘               └──────────────────────────┘

S2 and S3 reach ODOWN (quorum 2) and form a majority:
they promote R1. Now P and R1 are BOTH primaries.
Clients X keep writing to P; those writes are lost when the partition heals.

blocks.text:
This situation is called **split brain**. Sentinel prevents the minority side from starting a failover, but it cannot stop an isolated old primary from continuing to accept writes from clients that can still reach it. When the partition heals, the old primary is demoted to a replica and resyncs, which **discards** everything it accepted in the meantime.

You can bound the damage with the settings from the replication chapter:

blocks.code:
min-replicas-to-write 1
min-replicas-max-lag 10
blocks.title: redis.conf (primary and replicas)

blocks.text:
With these, an isolated primary stops accepting writes about 10 seconds after it loses its replicas, so the loss window is limited. The trade-off is that if all replicas fail, the primary also stops accepting writes. Even then the data loss is bounded, not eliminated.

Other limitations to keep in mind:

- **No sharding.** Dataset size and write throughput are limited to one node.
- **Failover is not instant.** Expect seconds of failed or retried commands, and design callers for it.
- **Writes can be lost.** Everything from the replication chapter still applies: replication is asynchronous.
- **Addresses must be stable and reachable.** Under Docker, NAT or Kubernetes, the addresses a Sentinel announces (`sentinel announce-ip`, `replica-announce-ip`) must be ones the clients can actually reach. By default Sentinel works with IP addresses; hostnames need `sentinel resolve-hostnames yes` (disabled by default), and `sentinel announce-hostnames yes` if you want hostnames reported to clients.
- **Sentinel can enter TILT mode.** If a Sentinel notices the system clock jumped or its own process was frozen for a long time, it temporarily stops acting (it still monitors but will not start failovers) so that a stalled machine does not trigger a bogus failover.
- **Sentinels need majority.** Losing two of three Sentinels means no automatic failover until one comes back, even though Redis itself keeps serving.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Run Sentinel on separate failure domains from the nodes it watches whenever you can, and test it. A failover you have never rehearsed (`SENTINEL failover`, or killing the primary in a staging environment) is a failover you do not know works. The Sentinel lab in the Hands-On Labs Part walks through exactly this.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between quorum and majority in Sentinel? Quorum is how many Sentinels must agree the primary is unreachable before it is marked objectively down and a failover is considered. Majority is how many Sentinels must vote to elect the leader that actually performs the failover; it is more than half of all Sentinels regardless of quorum. Detection needs the quorum, authorization to act needs the majority, which is why a minority partition can never promote a replica.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Sentinel gives one shard automatic failover and service discovery; it does not shard data.

- Run three or more Sentinels on different failure domains; quorum detects failure, majority authorizes failover.
- SDOWN is one Sentinel's opinion; ODOWN needs quorum; a leader is elected per configuration epoch.
- The new primary is chosen by replica priority, then replication offset, then run ID.
- Clients must be Sentinel-aware: configure Sentinel addresses and the master name, not the primary's IP.
- Split brain can still lose writes; bound it with `min-replicas-to-write` and `min-replicas-max-lag`.

Replication and Sentinel make Redis more available and add read capacity, but every node still holds the **whole** **dataset** and every write still goes to **one** primary. Three limits remain:

- **Memory.** The dataset must fit in the RAM of one machine (minus headroom for fork and copy-on-write during snapshots). A 400 GB dataset does not fit on a 256 GB server, and very large instances also make restarts, full syncs and backups painfully slow.
- **Write throughput.** One primary executes commands on essentially one core. A single Redis node can do very high operation counts per second, but there is a ceiling, and a few expensive commands can use it up.
- **Network bandwidth.** All traffic to the dataset flows through one network interface.

You can first move the ceiling by scaling **up**: a bigger machine, faster CPU, better network, tuned data structures. That is simple and often the right first move. When it stops being enough, you scale **out**: split the dataset into **shards**, each owned by a different primary, so memory, writes and bandwidth are spread across machines. The word for this is **sharding** (or partitioning).

### Three ways to shard

#### Client-side sharding

The application (or its client library) decides which Redis server holds a key, usually with a hash of the key. The servers know nothing about each other. The simplest form is `hash(key) mod N`, which breaks badly when N changes: adding one server moves almost every key. **Consistent hashing** reduces that to moving roughly `1/N` of the keys, and is what many older libraries used.

Client-side sharding costs nothing on the server side and adds no extra hop, but every client must share exactly the same view of the topology, there is no automatic failover, and resharding is your problem: you have to copy keys yourself and coordinate the switch.

#### Proxy-assisted sharding

A **proxy** sits between clients and the shards, speaks the Redis protocol, and routes each command to the right server. Clients talk to the proxy as if it were one big Redis. Well-known examples are Twemproxy (from Twitter) and Envoy's Redis filter. This keeps clients simple, but it adds a network hop (and latency), the proxy is one more component to run and make highly available, and proxies usually restrict multi-key commands, transactions and some other features.

#### Redis Cluster

Redis Cluster is the **built-in, server-side** solution. The nodes know about each other, divide the key space into **16384** **hash slots**, own subsets of the slots, detect failures and promote replicas by themselves, and tell clients (with redirections) when they asked the wrong node. There is no proxy. Clients are "smart": they learn which node owns which slots and talk directly to the right one.

### Hash slots instead of hashing servers

The key idea of Redis Cluster is an **indirection layer**. Instead of mapping keys directly to servers, keys map to one of 16384 **slots**, and slots map to servers:

blocks.code:
key ──CRC16, mod 16384──► slot (0..16383) ──table lookup──► node
Adding a node does not change any key's slot.
It only changes which node owns some of the slots.

blocks.text: This is what makes resizing practical. Moving data from node A to node B means moving a given slot (a bucket of keys), not rehashing everything. A key's slot never changes, so a slot is the unit of ownership, of migration and of failure.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Redis Cluster is built for scale and availability, not for transparency. Anything that touches several keys is only guaranteed to work when the keys are in the same slot. The next chapter spells out what that means for your code, and the key-design trick (hash tags) that fixes most cases.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Scale up first; scale out when memory, write throughput or bandwidth of one node is the limit.

- Sharding can be done in the client, in a proxy, or by the database (Redis Cluster).
- `hash(key) mod N` is a bad scheme because changing N remaps nearly every key.
- Redis Cluster adds an indirection: key → one of 16384 slots → node, so growing the cluster moves slots, not hashes.
- You trade away free multi-key operations in exchange for horizontal scale.

Redis Cluster is a set of Redis nodes that together present one logical database. Every node runs in cluster mode (`cluster-enabled yes`), keeps a full map of which node owns which slot, and talks to all other nodes over a dedicated TCP channel. There is no coordinator and no proxy; the nodes themselves form the control plane.

blocks.text: The slot of a key is computed as:

blocks.code: HASH_SLOT = CRC16(key) mod 16384

blocks.text: With three primaries, the usual split is 0 to 5460, 5461 to 10922 and 10923 to 16383. You can ask any node for the slot of a key:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:17001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:42:cart
(integer) 12984
127.0.0.1:17001> SET user:42:cart x
(error) MOVED 12984 127.0.0.1:17003
blocks.title: Which slot does a key belong to?

blocks.text:
The `SET` was sent to the node that does not own slot 12984, so it answers with a redirection (`MOVED`) rather than guessing. We will come back to that.

Why 16384 and not a larger number? Nodes exchange heartbeat messages that include the sender's slot ownership as a bitmap, and 16384 slots take 2 KB per message. The designers chose a number that keeps messages small and is still far more than the number of primaries (the practical upper limit is in the order of a thousand nodes) needed for even balancing.

#### Hash tags

By default the whole key is hashed. If the key contains a substring in curly braces, `{...}`, only the part between the **first** `{` and the **next** `}` is hashed, provided it is not empty. This lets you force related keys into the same slot:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:17001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {user:42}:cart
(integer) 15880
127.0.0.1:17001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT {user:42}:session
(integer) 15880
127.0.0.1:17001> CLUSTER KEYSLOT user:42:cart
(integer) 12984
blocks.title: Hash tags keep related keys together

blocks.text: With `{user:42}:cart` and `{user:42}:session` in the same slot, you can read both in one `MGET`, change both in a `MULTI`/`EXEC` transaction, or touch both from one Lua script. That is how ShopStream keeps a user's cart, session and recent-searches list atomically operable together.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Hash tags concentrate load. Everything sharing a tag lives on one node, so a tag like `{tenant:acme}` makes one primary hold, and serve, an entire big tenant, and a tag that is too coarse (`{cart}`) puts everything on one shard and silently destroys the benefit of the cluster. Tag by something with many distinct values (a user id, an order id), and keep the group of keys under the same tag small.

### Creating a cluster

A working cluster needs at least **three primaries** (so that a majority can agree a node has failed) and, for high availability, at least one replica per primary: six nodes. Each node needs a config like this:

blocks.code:
port 17001
cluster-enabled yes
cluster-config-file nodes-17001.conf
cluster-node-timeout 5000
appendonly yes
blocks.title: redis-17001.conf

blocks.text:
`cluster-config-file` is not something you write: the node maintains it automatically (it stores node ids, slots and epochs), and it must be writable and persistent. `cluster-node-timeout` is the central timeout, explained below. The default is 15000 ms; 5000 is a common production value that makes failover faster.

After starting all six, `redis-cli` can wire them up:

blocks.text:
A client may connect to any node and send any command. The node looks at the key's slot:

- If it owns the slot, it executes the command.
- Otherwise it replies `MOVED <slot> <ip>:<port>`, meaning "this slot is permanently served by that node". A cluster-aware client updates its slot table and re-sends the command there.
- During a migration of the slot, a node that has already moved a key away may reply `ASK <slot> <ip>:<port>`. This is a *temporary* redirect: the client sends `ASKING` followed by the command to the target node, **once**, and does **not** update its table.

`redis-cli` does not follow redirects unless you start it with `-c` (cluster mode):

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli -p 17001 SET foo bar
(error) MOVED 12182 127.0.0.1:17003
$ redis-cli -c -p 17001 SET foo bar
-> Redirected to slot [12182] located at 127.0.0.1:17003
OK
blocks.title: Without and with -c

blocks.text: Real clients (Lettuce, Jedis, Redisson, redis-py, go-redis, and so on) do this for you. They fetch the slot map when they connect (`CLUSTER SLOTS` or `CLUSTER SHARDS`), compute `CRC16(key) mod 16384` locally, and send each command directly to the owner, so in steady state there is no extra hop. They refresh the map when they see `MOVED` and, in better clients, periodically and on topology events. The Java clients Part shows how to turn on topology refresh in Lettuce, which matters during failovers and resharding.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A client that does not know Redis Cluster (a plain connection to one node) works only for the keys of that node and fails with `MOVED` on the rest. When someone says "Redis works locally but breaks in production", check that production is a cluster and that the client is cluster-aware.

### The cluster bus and gossip

Besides the normal port (6379 by default), every node opens a second TCP port, the **cluster bus**. By default it is the data port plus 10000 (6379 → 16379, as `17001` → `27001` above). It can be set with `cluster-port`. Nodes use a binary protocol on this bus to exchange heartbeat and gossip messages, to propagate configuration and slot changes, to run failure detection and to coordinate failovers. Clients must never connect to the bus port, but **both ports must be** **reachable between all nodes** (firewalls, security groups and Kubernetes network policies are the usual culprits when a new cluster will not form).

Gossip works as follows. Each node continuously sends `PING` to a few other nodes and answers with `PONG`; each message carries the sender's slots, its configuration epoch, its flags and information about a random sample of other nodes it knows. Over time every node learns about every other, and changes spread quickly without any central coordinator.

### Failure detection and failover

Failures are detected in two stages that resemble Sentinel's, but all done by the cluster's own nodes.

1. **PFAIL (possible failure).** A node that has not received a reply from another node for `cluster-node-timeout` milliseconds flags it as PFAIL. This is a local opinion.
2. **FAIL.** When a node learns, through gossip, that a **majority of primaries** consider the same node PFAIL, it marks the node FAIL and broadcasts that to the whole cluster. Only primaries count in this vote.

When a primary is flagged FAIL, its replicas start an election:

1. A replica waits a small delay that depends on how up to date it is (the one with the largest replication offset starts first) plus a random component.
2. It increments the cluster's current epoch and asks the primaries for votes. Each primary votes at most once per epoch.
3. When it collects votes from the **majority of primaries**, it promotes itself, takes over the old primary's slots, and announces the new configuration with a higher config epoch. Other nodes accept the configuration with the higher epoch.
4. The old primary, when it returns, sees that its slots have a newer owner and becomes a replica of the winner.

A replica that has been disconnected from its primary for too long is not allowed to fail over because its data would be too old. The limit is roughly `cluster-node-timeout × cluster-replica-validity-factor` (factor default 10) plus the replica ping period. Setting the factor to 0 means a replica always tries.

In the demo cluster, killing one primary (17003) leads, after about the node timeout plus the election, to this view; its replica (17006) is now a primary owning the slots:

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli -p 17001 CLUSTER NODES | awk '{print $2, $3, $8, $9}'
127.0.0.1:17001@27001 myself,master connected 0-5460
127.0.0.1:17002@27002 master connected 5461-10922
127.0.0.1:17004@27004 slave connected
127.0.0.1:17003@27003 master,fail disconnected
127.0.0.1:17005@27005 slave connected
127.0.0.1:17006@27006 master connected 10923-16383
blocks.title: After shutting down 17003 and waiting a few seconds

blocks.text:
The demo uses a 5 second node timeout, so detection and election took well under ten seconds. The output of a real run varies with timing, but the pattern is always the same: `master,fail` for the dead node, and the replica turned `master` with the slot range.

#### When the cluster stops accepting commands

The cluster as a whole is in state `ok` or `fail`:

- If a **majority of primaries** cannot talk to each other (a partition), the nodes on the minority side stop serving writes after the node timeout. They cannot be sure that the majority side has not promoted a replica, so they refuse rather than risk diverging.
- If some slot has no owner (a primary failed and had **no replica** that could take over), then by default (`cluster-require-full-coverage yes`) the **entire cluster** stops accepting commands, even for keys in healthy slots. Setting it to `no` lets the cluster serve the slots that are still covered, which is often the better trade-off for a cache but wrong for data you need to be consistent.
- `cluster-allow-reads-when-down` (default `no`) can let nodes serve reads while the cluster is marked failed. `cluster-allow-pubsubshard-when-down` (default `yes`) keeps sharded Pub/Sub working.

Like Sentinel, the cluster is asynchronously replicated, so writes acknowledged by a primary that then fails before they reach a replica are lost. `WAIT` helps in the same limited way. There is also a short window in a partition where a primary with clients on its side keeps accepting writes until the node timeout fires; `cluster-node-timeout` is therefore also the knob for how much you lose in such a split.

#### Replica migration

If one primary loses all its replicas while another has several, a spare replica can move automatically to the orphan. `cluster-migration-barrier` (default 1) is the minimum number of replicas a primary must keep before it donates one, and `cluster-allow-replica-migration` (default yes) controls whether nodes may do it. This gives you "N+1" resilience with fewer replicas than a full pair for every primary.

### What you give up: multi-key rules

Only commands whose keys are all in the **same slot** work across several keys. Otherwise the server returns:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:17001> MSET a 1 b 2
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot
127.0.0.1:17001> MSET {user:42}:a 1 {user:42}:b 2
OK
blocks.title: The CROSSSLOT error

blocks.text:
This applies to `MGET`, `MSET`, `DEL` with many keys, set operations (`SINTER`, `SUNION`...), `ZUNIONSTORE`, `RENAME`, `LMOVE`, and also to transactions (`MULTI`/`EXEC`) and to Lua scripts and functions: every key a script touches must be declared in `KEYS` and be in one slot. A script that builds key names at run time and touches another slot can fail or, worse, behave differently in a cluster than on your laptop.

The other differences you will meet:

- **Only database 0.** `SELECT` with another number is an error.
- **Commands that scan the key space work per node.** `KEYS`, `SCAN`, `DBSIZE`, `FLUSHALL` and `RANDOMKEY` act only on the node you ask; to cover everything you must run them on every primary (tools such as `redis-cli --cluster` `call` do that).
- **Pub/Sub.** A classic `PUBLISH` is propagated to every node over the bus, which does not scale with the node count. **Sharded Pub/Sub** (`SPUBLISH` / `SSUBSCRIBE`, since Redis 7.0) hashes the channel name to a slot and keeps messages within one shard.
- **Reading from replicas.** A replica redirects reads for its slots to the primary, unless the client first sends `READONLY` on that connection (Lettuce and Jedis can do this when you configure a read preference). Stale reads apply as in the replication chapter.
- **Big keys and hot slots.** A single key never splits across nodes, so a huge sorted set or a hot key stays on one primary. Sharding does not fix those; data modelling does.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Code that works on a standalone Redis and fails in a cluster is nearly always one of three things: a multi-key command across slots, a Lua script touching undeclared keys, or an assumption that `SCAN`/`KEYS` see the whole database. Develop and test against a cluster (Testcontainers can start one) if production is one.

### Using a cluster from Spring Boot

For application code, the cluster is mostly configuration. List a few seed nodes (the client discovers the rest) and the maximum number of redirects it should follow for one command:

blocks.code:
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      password: s3cr3t-change-me
      cluster:
        nodes:
          - 10.0.1.1:6379
          - 10.0.1.2:6379
          - 10.0.1.3:6379
        max-redirects: 3
blocks.title: application.yml

blocks.text: One detail will bite you in production: by default Lettuce reads the slot map once when it connects and refreshes it only when it needs to. If a primary fails and a replica takes over, or you reshard, a client with stale topology keeps sending commands to the old node. The remedy is to enable periodic and adaptive topology refresh:

blocks.title: RedisClusterConfig.java

blocks.text:
What to notice: `enablePeriodicRefresh` re-reads the topology on a timer, and `enableAllAdaptiveRefreshTriggers` makes the client refresh immediately when it sees a `MOVED` redirect, persistent reconnect failures and similar signs of a topology change. Together they shorten the time a client keeps asking the wrong node after a failover. The Lettuce chapter in the Java clients Part goes deeper on these options.

### A worked example: flash-sale stock in a cluster

ShopStream's flash sale decrements the stock of a SKU and records the reservation atomically. In a standalone Redis you would use two keys and one Lua script. In a cluster, both keys must share a slot, so they share a hash tag:

blocks.code:
-- KEYS[1] = {sku:1001}:stock   KEYS[2] = {sku:1001}:reserved:<orderId>
-- ARGV[1] = quantity           ARGV[2] = reservation TTL in seconds
local stock = tonumber(redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) or '0')
local qty = tonumber(ARGV[1])
if stock < qty then
  return 0
end
redis.call('DECRBY', KEYS[1], qty)
redis.call('SET', KEYS[2], qty, 'EX', tonumber(ARGV[2]))
return 1
blocks.title: reserve.lua

blocks.text:
Both keys contain `{sku:1001}`, so they hash to the same slot and the script is legal in a cluster. The design consequence is deliberate: all traffic for one SKU is served by one primary. For a million different SKUs that spreads evenly; for one extremely hot SKU it does not, and that single slot becomes the bottleneck (see the flash-sale pattern and project for ways to deal with it, for example splitting stock into several sub-counters, each with its own tag).

### Persistence, backups and configuration in a cluster

Each node persists independently. Use the same persistence policy you would use on a standalone node (see the persistence chapters in Part 4), on primaries and, usually, on replicas. A cluster backup is a set of per-node RDB files taken at roughly the same time; there is no single consistent snapshot of the whole cluster, so restoring means restoring every shard from backups of the same period. Treat `nodes.conf` as part of each node's state: keep it on persistent storage (a volume, not the container's temporary file system), otherwise a restarted node comes back with a new identity.

In containers and behind NAT, tell the node what address to advertise to its peers and to clients, with `cluster-announce-ip`, `cluster-announce-port`, `cluster-announce-bus-port`, or `cluster-announce-hostname` together with `cluster-preferred-endpoint-type` (default `ip`). If clients receive addresses in `MOVED` replies or in the topology that they cannot reach (for example container-internal IPs), every redirect will fail.

### CLUSTER commands you will meet

Topology: node ids, roles, slots, link state; SHARDS groups by shard

Introduce a node to the cluster
Make this node a replica of a primary
