blocks.text:
### Resharding with redis-cli

Moving slots between nodes while the cluster serves traffic is called **resharding**. `redis-cli --cluster reshard` does it interactively or from the command line:

blocks.code:
$ redis-cli --cluster reshard 127.0.0.1:17001 \
    --cluster-from all --cluster-to 6c12bd9ac044ca22cef2c4047c22c16143bc779d \
    --cluster-slots 100 --cluster-yes
...
Moving slot 10970 from 127.0.0.1:17006 to 127.0.0.1:17001:
Moving slot 10971 from 127.0.0.1:17006 to 127.0.0.1:17001:
blocks.title: Move 100 slots from all primaries to 17001

blocks.text:
For each slot, the tool marks it as migrating on the source and importing on the target (`CLUSTER SETSLOT`), copies the keys with `MIGRATE` in batches, and finally assigns the slot to the new owner. During that time, a request for a key not yet moved is answered by the source, and a request for a key already moved gets an `ASK` redirect. The next chapter covers the improved mechanism in Redis 8.4 and the day-to-day operations of growing and shrinking a cluster.

#### redis-cli --cluster at a glance

rows: Build a new cluster from empty nodes (`--cluster-replicas N` adds N replicas per primary)
Verify all slots are covered and that nodes agree on the configuration
Short summary: keys and slots per primary
Move a chosen number of slots from some nodes to another
Spread slots evenly (or by `--cluster-weight`); `--cluster-simulate` previews it
Add a node (as primary, or as replica with `--cluster-slave`) / remove an empty node
Repair open slots after an interrupted migration
Run one command on every node
blocks.caption: The subcommands you will use most.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does Redis Cluster decide where a key lives, and what happens if a client asks the wrong node? It computes `CRC16(key) mod 16384` to get a slot (using only the `{hash tag}` if the key has one), and each primary owns a set of slots. A node that does not own the slot replies `MOVED slot host:port`, and a cluster-aware client updates its slot map and retries there; during a slot migration the source may reply `ASK`, which is a one-off redirect. Multi-key operations only work when all keys are in the same slot, which is why hash tags exist.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does a Redis Cluster need at least three primaries? Failure of a primary is declared and a replica is elected by a majority of primaries. With one or two primaries there is no meaningful majority that survives the loss of a node.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: ShopStream keeps `{user:ID}:cart`, `{user:ID}:session` and `{user:ID}:recent` under one hash tag so the cart service can read and update them in one Lua script, while product caches use plain keys (`product:ID`) that spread evenly across all slots. Each of the six nodes in the cluster runs on a different host, with every replica in a different zone from its primary.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
A key's slot is `CRC16(key) mod 16384`; hash tags in `{}` force related keys into the same slot.

- Slots are the unit of ownership and migration; three primaries minimum, plus replicas for failover.
- Smart clients cache the slot map; `MOVED` updates it, `ASK` is a one-time redirect during migration.
- Failure detection: PFAIL by one node, FAIL by a majority of primaries, replica election by a majority of primaries.
- By default the whole cluster stops if any slot is uncovered (`cluster-require-full-coverage yes`).
- Cluster means no cross-slot multi-key commands, only database 0, and per-node `SCAN`/`KEYS`.

sections.title: Atomic slot migration and operating a cluster

blocks.text:
A cluster is not finished when `cluster_state:ok` appears. Data grows, traffic shifts, hardware ages and versions change, so you will add and remove nodes, move slots, fail over on purpose and upgrade while the system serves traffic. This chapter covers the newer tools (atomic slot migration in Redis 8.4, per-slot statistics in 8.2) and the routine operations.

### How classic slot migration works, and what is wrong with it

Until Redis 8.4, moving a slot meant key-by-key copying driven from outside the servers (by `redis-cli --cluster` `reshard` or your own tooling):

1. Mark the slot `IMPORTING` on the target and `MIGRATING` on the source (`CLUSTER SETSLOT`).
2. List keys of the slot (`CLUSTER GETKEYSINSLOT`) and move batches with `MIGRATE`, which serialises a key, sends it, and deletes it from the source.
3. Once the slot is empty, tell everyone the target owns it (`CLUSTER SETSLOT ... NODE`).

It works and it is online, but it has well-known rough edges. While the slot is half moved, the keys of that slot are split across two nodes, so a multi-key command on keys of that slot may fail with `TRYAGAIN`, and clients see `ASK` redirections for a while. A very large key is moved as one blocking `MIGRATE`, which stalls the source for as long as it takes. And because the whole process is driven by an external tool, a crash of that tool in the middle leaves "open slots" that you repair with `redis-cli --cluster fix`.

### Atomic slot migration (Redis 8.4)

Redis Open Source 8.4 introduces **atomic slot migration** with a new command, `CLUSTER MIGRATION`. The idea is to move a whole slot range as one unit of work, driven by the servers rather than by an external script, and to switch ownership in a single step, so clients are not exposed to a half-moved slot.

You run the command on the **destination primary**, naming the slot ranges to pull:

blocks.code:
CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT 0 1000 2000 3000
CLUSTER MIGRATION STATUS ALL
CLUSTER MIGRATION STATUS ID 24cf41718b20f7f05901743dffc40bc9b15db339
CLUSTER MIGRATION CANCEL ID 24cf41718b20f7f05901743dffc40bc9b15db339
CLUSTER MIGRATION CANCEL ALL

blocks.text:
`IMPORT start-slot end-slot [start-slot end-slot ...]` accepts several ranges (above: slots 0 to 1000 and 2000 to 3000) and returns a **task id**. The destination then takes a snapshot of those slots from their current owner, receives the writes made in the meantime as a stream, and, when the remaining stream is small enough, the source briefly pauses writes to those slots and hands ownership over. After the handoff the source drops the data of the migrated slots.

`STATUS` lists tasks (all, or one by id) with fields such as `id`, `slots`, `source`, `dest`, `operation`, `state`, `last_error`, `retries`, `create_time`, `start_time`, `end_time` and `write_pause_ms`. A successful task shows state `completed` and an empty `last_error`. `CANCEL` stops one task or all of them; note that cancelling on the source node does not stop the destination, which keeps retrying until it is cancelled there as well, so cancel on both.

Two settings control the handoff:

rows: When the remaining stream is below this, the source pauses writes and hands off
Longest the source pauses writes; if the destination has not taken over by then, the source resumes and treats the migration as failed
blocks.caption: Atomic slot migration settings.

blocks.text:
Things to be aware of, taken from the current documentation:

- While a migration is importing or trimming, keys in slots a node does not own may be filtered out of `KEYS`, `SCAN`, `RANDOMKEY`, `CLUSTER GETKEYSINSLOT`, `DBSIZE` and `CLUSTER COUNTKEYSINSLOT`, while `INFO KEYSPACE` still shows the real number of keys, including those being imported. Do not alarm if the two disagree for a short time.
- Search commands (`FT.SEARCH`, `FT.AGGREGATE`, `FT.CURSOR`, `FT.HYBRID`) and some time series multi-key queries (`TS.MGET`, `TS.MRANGE`, `TS.MREVRANGE`, `TS.QUERYINDEX`) may return partial results or duplicates while a migration is in progress.
- The command is available in Redis Open Source 8.4 and later; the documentation lists it as not supported for the Standard and Active-Active offerings of Redis Software and Redis Cloud. Check the version of every node before you rely on it, and check whether your version of `redis-cli --cluster reshard` uses it or the classic key-by-key path.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The honest summary: atomic slot migration removes the long half-migrated state and the dependence on an external driver. It does not make resharding free. Moving data still costs CPU, memory and network on both nodes, and a short write pause on the migrating slots is part of the design (look at `write_pause_ms` in `STATUS`). Do migrations at a quiet time and watch latency.

### Finding what to move: CLUSTER SLOT-STATS (Redis 8.2)

Balanced slot counts do not mean balanced load. One slot can hold a hot key or a huge sorted set. Redis 8.2 added `CLUSTER SLOT-STATS` to report per-slot usage on the node you ask:

blocks.code:
CLUSTER SLOT-STATS SLOTSRANGE 0 100
CLUSTER SLOT-STATS ORDERBY CPU-USEC LIMIT 10 DESC

blocks.text:
You pick exactly one of two forms. `SLOTSRANGE start end` returns the stats for an inclusive range of slots in ascending slot order. `ORDERBY metric [LIMIT n] [ASC | DESC]` sorts all slots by a metric so that the heaviest are first. The metrics are `KEY-COUNT`, `CPU-USEC`, `MEMORY-BYTES`, `NETWORK-BYTES-IN` and `NETWORK-BYTES-OUT`. Everything except `KEY-COUNT` needs `cluster-slot-stats-enabled yes` in the configuration (it adds a little accounting overhead).

A practical workflow: find the node with the highest CPU or memory, ask it for the top slots by `CPU-USEC` or `MEMORY-BYTES`, and migrate those slots to a quieter primary (with `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT` on 8.4 or `reshard` before that). If a single slot dominates, moving it only relocates the problem; the real fix is in the data model (split the hot key, remove a hash tag that is too coarse).

### Everyday operations

#### Adding a node

1. Start the new node with `cluster-enabled yes` and the same security settings (`requirepass`/`masterauth`, ACLs, TLS) as the others.
2. Join it. As an empty primary: `redis-cli --cluster add-node 10.0.1.9:6379 10.0.1.1:6379` (new node first, then any existing node). As a replica of a specific primary: add `--cluster-slave --cluster-master-id <node-id>`; without the id, the tool picks a primary with the fewest replicas.
3. An empty primary owns no slots and serves nothing. Give it slots with `reshard`, with `rebalance` `--cluster-use-empty-masters`, or with `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT`.

#### Rebalancing

`redis-cli --cluster rebalance <host:port>` moves slots until each primary's share is within a threshold of the average (default 2 percent), optionally weighted by `--cluster-weight node=weight`, and `--cluster-simulate` shows what it would do without doing it. Always simulate first. It balances slot counts, not load, so combine it with `SLOT-STATS` where load is uneven.

#### Removing a node

A replica can be removed at once. A primary must own **no slots** first, so reshard its slots away, check with `--cluster` `check`, and only then run `redis-cli --cluster del-node <host:port> <node-id>`. The tool tells the other nodes to forget the node and resets it. If you simply switch off a node without this, the others keep it in their tables as failed, and you must remove it with `CLUSTER FORGET <node-id>` on every other node (`redis-cli --cluster call ... cluster` `forget <id>` can do this).

#### Planned failover

To take a primary out for maintenance without losing a write, log in to **its replica** and run:

blocks.code:
127.0.0.1:17004> CLUSTER FAILOVER
OK
blocks.title: Planned failover

blocks.text:
The default form is coordinated: the replica asks the primary to pause clients, waits until it has processed every write, starts an election and takes over, and the old primary becomes its replica. Variants: `CLUSTER FAILOVER FORCE` skips the primary's cooperation (use it when the primary is unreachable but not yet marked failed) and `CLUSTER FAILOVER` `TAKEOVER` takes over without any election and without agreement, a last-resort tool that can lose writes and should be used by an operator who knows why.

#### Rolling upgrade

1. Upgrade the **replicas** one at a time (stop, replace binary, start, wait until `master_link_status:up` and the cluster is `ok`).
2. For each primary, run `CLUSTER FAILOVER` on its upgraded replica, so the upgraded node becomes primary.
3. Upgrade the old primaries, now replicas.
4. Verify with `redis-cli --cluster check` and `CLUSTER INFO`.

Read the release notes for every version you cross (especially from Redis 7 to 8) and test on a staging cluster first. Do not run mixed-version clusters longer than needed and avoid using new features until all nodes are upgraded. The upgrades chapter in the operations Part has the full checklist.

### Health checks and common problems

Watch `cluster_state`, `cluster_slots_fail`, `cluster_slots_pfail` and `cluster_known_nodes` in `CLUSTER INFO`, plus replication lag per shard and `redis-cli --cluster check` in a scheduled job. The table shows the frequent causes of trouble.

rows: A slot is uncovered (primary and its replicas lost) or no majority of primaries is reachable
`CLUSTER NODES`, `--cluster check`; restore a node; consider `cluster-require-full-coverage no` for caches
Bus port blocked, wrong announced IP behind NAT or in containers
`cluster-node-timeout` too low for network or GC-like pauses, slow commands blocking a node
Look at `SLOWLOG`, latency, raise the timeout moderately
Client not caching slot map, or topology refresh disabled
Use a cluster-aware client, enable refresh
Replica data too old (validity factor) or `cluster-replica-no-failover yes`
blocks.caption: Cluster symptoms and first checks.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never copy a node's `nodes.conf` (the file named by `cluster-config-file`) to another node or restore an old one into a running cluster: node ids and epochs are in it, and duplicates confuse the whole cluster. To replace a failed node, start a fresh node, add it as a replica of the primary, or let it resync.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Atomic slot migration (8.4) moves slot ranges with `CLUSTER MIGRATION IMPORT`, run on the destination primary, and avoids the long half-moved state of classic `MIGRATE`.

- `CLUSTER SLOT-STATS` (8.2) shows per-slot key count and, if enabled, CPU, memory and network use, to find what to move.
- Add nodes empty, then give them slots; remove nodes only after emptying them.
- Use `CLUSTER FAILOVER` on a replica for planned, lossless switchovers and rolling upgrades.
- Test everything on a staging cluster and know the cluster-bus ports before you need them.

You now know four ways to run Redis: a single node, a primary with replicas, a primary with replicas and Sentinel, and Redis Cluster. They are not stages you must climb in order. Each is a trade between simplicity, availability, capacity and what your application has to know. Choosing well usually means choosing the simplest one that meets your requirements.

Start with four questions:

1. **What happens to the business if Redis is gone for a minute? For an hour?** (Availability.)
2. **What happens if the last few seconds of writes are lost?** (Durability and consistency.)
3. **Will the data fit in one machine's memory with headroom, and can one primary handle the writes?** (Capacity.)
4. **Which features does the application need that a cluster restricts?** (Multi-key operations, Lua, transactions, database numbers.)

### The four topologies

rows: Simplest; lowest latency; full command set
One machine's memory and one core
Node down = Redis down until restart or restore
Copy of data; read scaling; offloads backups
Same as one node for memory and writes
Promote by hand; clients need a new address
Seconds of errors during failover; async replication can lose recent writes; split brain possible
Memory and write throughput scale out; automatic failover per shard
A shard without any replica makes its slots unavailable; minority partitions stop; async loss as above
blocks.caption: Topologies and their failure modes.

blocks.text:
#### When a single node is the right answer

Many production systems should stay here for a long time. If the data is a few gigabytes, the load is well below what one core can do, and the data is a rebuildable cache, one node with sensible persistence (or none), monitoring and a documented restore procedure is a legitimate design. Redis restarts quickly with RDB, and the application may already tolerate a cold cache. Do not buy complexity you do not need.

#### Primary + replicas

Adding one replica turns "lost the machine" from a data-loss event into a "promote and repoint clients" event. Without Sentinel the promotion is manual, which can be acceptable for internal tools and batch systems where a human is around. It also gives you somewhere to take backups and run slow analytic scans without hurting the primary.

#### Sentinel

This is the standard answer for "I need automatic failover and my data fits in one node". The cost is three Sentinel processes, a Sentinel-aware client and the discipline to test failovers. Throughput is still bound to a single primary: you add read capacity with replicas, not write capacity.

#### Cluster

Choose Cluster when one node cannot hold the dataset or serve the writes, or when you want failover without extra processes. Count the costs honestly: a minimum of six nodes for a sane setup, a cluster-aware client, hash tags in your key design, and the restrictions on cross-slot operations. If your code uses scripts, transactions or set intersections across arbitrary keys, you will spend real effort adapting it.

### A decision walk-through

blocks.code:
Does the data (plus ~50% headroom for fork) fit on one node,
and can one primary take the write load?
  │
  ├── yes ── Can you accept manual recovery (minutes to hours)?
  │            ├── yes ── single node (+ backups), or primary + replica
  │            └── no  ── primary + replicas + Sentinel (3 sentinels)
  │
  └── no  ── Redis Cluster (3+ primaries, each with 1+ replica)
             (or shard by function first: sessions on one Redis, catalogue
              cache on another, and keep each on the simplest topology)

blocks.text:
The last line of the diagram is important: **splitting by purpose** is often a better first step than a cluster. If ShopStream's session store, catalogue cache and rate limiter share one Redis, they compete for memory and one noisy workload (a cache full of big product JSON) can evict the others' keys. Separate instances per role, each with its own `maxmemory`, eviction policy and persistence setting, are often simpler than one giant cluster and isolate failures.

### Sizing rules of thumb

- **Memory headroom.** A primary that forks for RDB or AOF rewrite can use significantly more memory while it takes writes (copy-on-write). Plan `maxmemory` well below the machine's RAM; a common starting point is to leave a large fraction free if the write rate is high. The operations Part has the arithmetic.
- **Replicas need the same memory as the primary**, plus buffers for the replication stream.
- **Cluster shard size.** Smaller shards (for example 10 to 25 GB per primary) restart, sync and migrate faster than a few giant ones. More shards add more nodes and more cross-slot restrictions, so this is a balance, not a rule.
- **Three of everything in different failure domains.** Three Sentinels, primaries and replicas of one shard in different zones or racks.

rows: Shard fails over, small write loss possible
Survives if replicas and a Sentinel majority are in other zones
Survives if each shard has a replica elsewhere and a primary majority survives
Replicated on that shard (and others if sent to all), backups only
blocks.caption: What a topology protects you from.

blocks.text:
### Moving from one topology to the next

Topologies change as a system grows, so choose one you can leave. Moving from a single node to primary-plus-replica or Sentinel is easy: add replicas, add Sentinels, switch the client configuration. Moving to Cluster is a real migration, because the data model must satisfy the same-slot rules and the client must change.

A pragmatic plan looks like this:

1. **Make your key design cluster-ready before you need a cluster.** Put related keys under a hash tag now (`{user:42}:cart`), declare every key a Lua script touches in `KEYS`, and avoid `KEYS`/`SCAN`-based global logic. These habits cost nothing on a standalone node.
2. **Test against a cluster early**, for example with Testcontainers or a docker-compose cluster, so that cross-slot errors appear in the build and not in production.
3. **Load the cluster in parallel.** For caches, simply deploy the cluster, switch the application over and let it warm up. For data you cannot rebuild, copy it with a migration tool or your own pipeline (scan the old instance, write to the cluster through a cluster-aware client), run both for a while, then cut over.
4. **Keep the rollback path** until the new topology has run through a real failover.

For caches, rebuilding is often the best migration; for state that lives only in Redis, treat the move like any database migration, with a rehearsal and a verified rollback.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How do you decide between Sentinel and Cluster? If the dataset and write load fit on one primary and you want automatic failover, use replication with Sentinel: simpler, full command set, no key-design restrictions. If memory or write throughput exceeds one node, or you want to grow horizontally, use Cluster and accept same-slot rules, hash tags and a cluster-aware client. Neither removes the possibility of losing recently acknowledged writes in a failover.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Pick the simplest topology that meets availability, durability and capacity needs.

- Single node and primary-plus-replica are respectable choices for rebuildable data.
- Sentinel adds automatic failover for one shard; Cluster adds scale-out and per-shard failover.
- Separating workloads by purpose is often better than one big shared cluster.
- Every topology uses asynchronous replication, so none is a zero-loss guarantee.

Everything so far assumed that all nodes sit close to one another, with network round trips measured in fractions of a millisecond. Moving data between regions changes the picture. A round trip between continents takes tens to well over a hundred milliseconds, links fail more often, and the speed of light is not negotiable. This chapter gives an overview of the options and trade-offs, then of managed services. It is deliberately descriptive: product features and names change quickly, so check your provider's current documentation before you decide.

### Why go beyond one region

- **Latency for users.** A user in another continent should not pay 150 ms for every cache read.
- **Disaster recovery.** A whole region can become unavailable.
- **Data residency.** Some data must stay in a particular jurisdiction.

These goals pull in different directions, and the right design depends on which one matters most.

### Patterns

#### Independent caches per region

The simplest and most common: each region runs its own Redis, populated from the source of truth in that region (or from a regional read replica of the database). Nothing is replicated between Redis instances. A cache miss in region B costs a database read, not a cross-region call. This works well for caches, sessions that are tied to a region, and rate limits that can be per region.

#### Cross-region replica (disaster recovery or read locality)

A replica in another region is set up with ordinary replication (or the managed equivalent). Reads in that region are fast but stale by at least the network latency plus replication lag; writes still go to the single primary region, so remote writers pay the round trip. For disaster recovery you promote the remote replica manually or with orchestration. Because replication is asynchronous, the recovery point is "whatever had arrived", and you should measure that lag. Putting Sentinel or Cluster members across regions makes the failure detection timeouts and quorum maths harder, since a long inter-region latency spike looks like a failure; this is usually avoided in favour of per-region clusters plus an explicit failover process.

#### Active-active

In an active-active (multi-writer) design, every region accepts writes to the same logical dataset and changes are merged between regions. Merging requires conflict resolution, and a general-purpose Redis command stream cannot be merged naively (what is the result if two regions `INCR` the same counter, or `SET` the same key, at the same moment?). Active-active products solve this with **conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs)** that define merge rules per data type, such as counters that add and sets that union. Redis offers this in its commercial products (Redis Software and Redis Cloud); it is not part of Redis Open Source. The consequence for your design is that you must think in terms of eventual consistency and mergeable operations, and some commands and patterns (for example lock-style compare-and-set across regions) do not have a meaningful active-active meaning.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: **A distributed lock across regions is almost never what you want.** Round-trip times make lock acquisition slow, and asynchronous replication means two regions can both believe they hold it. Keep locks regional, or move the critical decision into the database that is the system of record.

### Managed Redis services

Running Redis well (patching, failover, backups, monitoring, scaling) is real work, and most cloud providers sell it as a service. In general terms, they fall into these groups:

- **Managed open-source-compatible caches.** The provider runs Redis-compatible nodes for you, with a replication group or a cluster-mode option, automatic failover across availability zones, snapshots and a console. Amazon ElastiCache, Azure Cache for Redis (and its successors) and Google Cloud Memorystore are examples of this category.
- **Durable, multi-AZ Redis-compatible databases.** Some services, for example Amazon MemoryDB, keep a multi-AZ transaction log so that acknowledged writes survive a node failure, aiming for use as a primary database rather than a cache. They trade some write latency for that durability.
- **Redis's own cloud and software.** Redis Cloud and Redis Software add features such as active-active geo-distribution and tiering, with their own operational model.
- **Serverless variants.** Some providers offer pay-per-request or auto-scaling flavours that hide the node topology.

Because offerings change, here is what to evaluate rather than what any provider says today:

rows: Which engine and version is it (Redis Open Source, Valkey, or a compatible implementation)?
Command and feature availability (for example Redis 8 data types, Functions, newest commands) may lag or differ
Decides whether your client must be cluster-aware and how multi-key commands behave
What is the failover time and the write-loss guarantee?
Sets your application's retry and idempotency requirements
Which commands and configuration settings are restricted?
Providers commonly block `CONFIG`, `DEBUG`, `MODULE` and others; some modules or data types may be absent
Cache-only or durable; restore time and cross-region copy
Security posture; latency from your compute
Pricing model (instance-hour, per GB, per request, data transfer)
Cross-zone and cross-region traffic is often a significant part of the bill

#### Cost and latency trade-offs

Memory is the main cost driver: RAM is expensive, so keeping a large cold dataset in Redis costs far more than in a database. Replicas multiply the memory bill. Cross-zone replication traffic and cross-region transfer are usually billed. Latency changes with placement: a client in another availability zone typically pays a fraction of a millisecond more per round trip than one in the same zone, which matters when an application makes many sequential calls; use pipelining and keep chatty components close to Redis.

### A regional disaster recovery runbook

Whatever product you use, a cross-region recovery plan should be written down and rehearsed. A minimal runbook for a primary region lost to an outage has these parts:

1. **Decide and declare.** Who may declare a regional failover, and on what evidence (not on one failed health check). A premature promotion is worse than a short wait, because it creates two divergent datasets.
2. **Fence the old region.** Make sure the old primary cannot accept writes if it comes back (firewall, `REPLICAOF` to the new primary, or shutting it down) to prevent split brain across regions.
3. **Promote the remote replica** (`REPLICAOF NO ONE`, or the provider's promotion call) and note the replication offset or time you recovered to. Writes after that point are lost; record the window for the incident report.
4. **Redirect traffic**: DNS, service discovery or configuration. Remember DNS caching and client reconnect behaviour.
5. **Rebuild redundancy**: add replicas to the new primary and, later, set up the reverse direction for fail-back.
6. **Reconcile**: compare against the system of record and replay or repair anything that matters.

The recovery point is bounded by replication lag at the moment of failure and the recovery time by how automated these steps are. Measure both in a drill; do not guess.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: For ShopStream, a sensible shape is a managed or self-run replicated Redis per region for sessions and catalogue cache, the catalogue and orders in a regional database, and no attempt to share a Redis dataset across regions. Cross-region concerns (inventory, orders) are handled in the database or by event streams between regions, not by stretching Redis.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Multi-region adds latency and failure modes; independent regional caches are the simplest and most robust pattern.

- A cross-region replica gives local reads and disaster recovery, with stale reads and asynchronous loss.
- Active-active needs CRDT-style merge semantics and is a feature of Redis commercial products, not Redis Open Source.
- Managed services remove operations work but vary in version, features, restrictions and cost; check them against your needs.
- Avoid cross-region locks and cross-region synchronous assumptions.
